relationship: prophetic messages directed to Nineveh
rationale: Nahum identifies his book as an oracle concerning Nineveh. Jonah receives the Lord's command to go to that named city and proclaim because its wickedness has come before Him. Both explicitly identify Nineveh as the destination of prophetic address.
source_text: An oracle concerning Nineveh; the book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite.

target_units.text: The word of the Lord came to Jonah, the son of Amittai, saying:
“Rise and go to Nineveh, the great city, and proclaim in it, for the outcry of its wickedness has come up to Me.”

relationship: the Lord explicitly described as jealous
rationale: Nahum calls the Lord a jealous and avenging God. Exodus likewise names Him Jealous and calls Him a jealous God when forbidding worship of another god. The shared description is explicit, while Nahum emphasizes vengeance upon adversaries.
source_text: The Lord is a jealous and avenging God, the Lord avenging with fury, the Lord avenging Himself on His adversaries, and He Himself removes His enemies.

target_units.text: You shall not bow down to another god, for the Lord God, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God.

relationship: vengeance and judgment belonging to the Lord
rationale: Nahum presents the Lord avenging Himself upon adversaries and removing enemies. Deuteronomy likewise places repayment in His day of vengeance and announces His judgment, while also speaking of concern for His weakened servants.
source_text: The Lord is a jealous and avenging God, the Lord avenging with fury, the Lord avenging Himself on His adversaries, and He Himself removes His enemies.

target_units.text: In the day of vengeance I will repay, in the season when their foot shall slip; for the day of their destruction is near, and the things prepared for you are at hand.
For the Lord shall judge His people, and be moved concerning His servants; for He saw them weakened, and failing under assault, and exhausted.

relationship: patience joined to the refusal to acquit guilt
rationale: Nahum places the Lord's patience beside the declaration that He certainly will not acquit. Exodus likewise describes Him as slow to anger and merciful while saying that He does not cleanse the guilty. Neither passage makes patience an absence of judgment.
source_text: The Lord is patient, and His strength is great; the Lord certainly will not acquit. His way is in consummation and shaking; clouds are the dust of His feet.

target_units.text: The Lord passed before him and proclaimed, “The Lord God, compassionate and merciful, slow to anger, abundant in mercy and true,

preserving righteousness and showing mercy to thousands, taking away lawlessness, injustice, and sins, yet not cleansing the guilty, bringing the fathers’ lawlessness upon children and children’s children to the third and fourth generation.”

relationship: the Lord's threat dries seas and rivers
rationale: Nahum says the Lord threatens the sea and dries it, making rivers desolate. Isaiah likewise describes His threat making the sea desolate and turning rivers to deserts. Both expressly connect desiccated waters with His power.
source_text: He threatens the sea and dries it up, and makes all the rivers desolate. Bashan and Carmel have dwindled, and Lebanon’s flowering things have failed.

target_units.text: Why did I come when no person was there, call when no one obeyed? Is My hand not strong enough to rescue? Am I not able to deliver? Behold, by My threat I will make the sea desolate and turn rivers to deserts; their fish will dry up for lack of water and die in thirst.

relationship: the Lord makes the sea dry
rationale: Nahum describes the Lord drying the sea. Exodus narrates a particular occasion when He drives the sea back and makes it dry so that Israel can pass through. The historical scene supplies an explicit example of power over the sea, without identifying it as Nahum's only referent.
source_text: He threatens the sea and dries it up, and makes all the rivers desolate. Bashan and Carmel have dwindled, and Lebanon’s flowering things have failed.

target_units.text: Moses stretched out his hand over the sea. The Lord drove the sea back with a violent south wind all night and made the sea dry. The water was split.
The sons of Israel entered the midst of the sea on dry ground, and the water was a wall for them on the right and a wall on the left.

relationship: mountains and earth shaken before the Lord
rationale: Nahum describes mountains and hills shaken and the earth recoiling before the Lord. The psalm likewise depicts mountains and hills moving and expressly says the earth was shaken before Him. The images concern creation's response to His presence.
source_text: Mountains shook before Him and hills were shaken; the whole earth recoiled before Him, and all who dwell in it.

target_units.text: The mountains skipped like rams, and the hills like lambs of sheep.
What is it with you, sea, that you fled, and with you, Jordan, that you withdrew backward?
Mountains, that you skipped like rams, and hills, like lambs of sheep?
Before the Lord the earth was shaken, before the God of Jacob,

relationship: the question of standing before divine appearance and melting imagery
rationale: Nahum asks who can stand before the Lord's anger and says His fury melts rulers. Malachi likewise asks who will stand at the coming appearance and describes smelting and melting the sons of Levi. The shared question and melting imagery have different subjects and purposes in their respective contexts.
source_text: Who will stand before His anger? Who will resist His furious wrath? His fury melts rulers, and rocks were crushed before Him.

target_units.text: And who will endure the day of his entrance? Or who will stand at his appearance? For he enters like a smelting fire and like launderers’ herb.

He will sit, smelting and purifying as with silver and gold. He will cleanse the sons of Levi and melt them like gold and silver, and they will be those who bring a sacrifice to the Lord in righteousness.

relationship: the Lord's goodness to those who wait for Him
rationale: Nahum says the Lord is good to those waiting for Him in affliction. Lamentations likewise explicitly calls Him good to those who wait for Him and describes enduring quietly for His salvation. The connection preserves Nahum's waiting language rather than importing a stronghold image.
source_text: The Lord is good to those who wait for Him in a day of affliction, and He knows those who revere Him.

target_units.text: The Lord is good to those who wait for Him, to the soul that will seek Him as good
and will endure and be quiet for the Lord’s salvation.

relationship: an overwhelming advance represented by powerful waters
rationale: Nahum pictures an advancing flood making an end of opponents. Isaiah likewise pictures strong river water advancing over walls and filling the country, explicitly identifying its force with the Assyrian king. The image is shared, while Assyria's role and the people threatened differ.
source_text: With an advancing flood He will make a complete end of those who rise up, and darkness will pursue His enemies.

target_units.text: therefore, behold, the Lord brings up against you the river’s strong and abundant water—the king of the Assyrians and his glory. He will ascend every ravine of yours and walk over every wall of yours,
and he will remove from Judea a person able to lift a head or someone strong enough to accomplish anything. His encampment will fill the breadth of your country. God is with us.”

relationship: counsel opposed to God cannot endure
rationale: Nahum asks what is devised against the Lord before announcing His complete end. Isaiah likewise says that the Lord will scatter devised counsel and that the spoken word will not endure. The connection concerns failed opposition, not a claim that Isaiah repeats Nahum's statement about vengeance twice.
source_text: What do you devise against the Lord? He will make a complete end; He will not exact vengeance twice upon the same thing in affliction.

target_units.text: Whatever counsel you devise, the Lord will scatter; whatever word you speak will certainly not endure for you, because the Lord God is with us.

relationship: destructive burning pictured through vegetation
rationale: Nahum compares consumption with an entwining thorn-vine and dry stubble. Isaiah describes burning against glory and woodland consumed like grass, extending to mountains, hills and forests. Both use combustible vegetation to picture devastating judgment, with different plants named.
source_text: For it will be laid waste to their foundation, consumed like an entwining thorn-vine and like stubble full of dryness.

target_units.text: And it will not be so; rather, the Lord Sabaoth will send dishonor against your honor, and against your glory a burning fire will burn.
Israel’s light will become fire, and He will sanctify him in burning fire and consume the woodland like grass. On that day,
the mountains, hills and forests will be extinguished, and it will consume from soul to flesh. The one fleeing will be like someone fleeing from a burning flame.

relationship: same-chapter recurrence of schemes against the Lord
rationale: Nahum 1:11 identifies a scheme devising evil in opposition to the Lord. The earlier question in 1:9 asks what is devised against Him and announces His response. The repeated devising language develops the same accusation within the chapter.
source_text: From you will come a scheme, devising evil things in opposition to the Lord.

target_units.text: What do you devise against the Lord? He will make a complete end; He will not exact vengeance twice upon the same thing in affliction.

relationship: the Lord's authority over many waters
rationale: Nahum introduces the Lord as the One who rules many waters. The psalm likewise places the Lord over many waters and His voice over the waters. The shared description identifies the authority of the speaker, without making the subsequent threats identical.
source_text: Thus says the Lord who rules many waters: Even so they will be separated, and your report will no longer be heard.

target_units.text: The Lord’s voice is over the waters; the God of glory thundered; the Lord is over many waters.

relationship: release from an oppressor's rod and yoke
rationale: Nahum promises to crush his rod away and tear apart bonds. Isaiah tells the people not to fear the Assyrian's rod and promises the removal and destruction of his yoke. Both describe liberation through the removal of instruments of oppression.
source_text: And now I will crush his rod away from you and tear apart your bonds.

target_units.text: Therefore thus says the Lord Sabaoth: “Do not fear the Assyrians, My people dwelling in Zion, because he will strike you with a rod; for I bring a blow upon you to see Egypt’s way.
For yet a little while, and the wrath will cease, but My anger will be against their counsel.”
God will rouse action against them according to Midian’s blow in a place of affliction, and His anger on the way by the sea, toward the way by Egypt.
On that day his fear will be removed from you and his yoke from your shoulder, and the yoke will be destroyed from your shoulders.

relationship: the Lord destroys carved images
rationale: Nahum announces the destruction of carved and cast images from the house of the addressed one's god. Micah likewise announces the Lord's destruction of carved images and pillars and the end of bowing to human handiwork. The shared action concerns images, while the addressed settings differ.
source_text: The Lord will command concerning you: No more will be sown from your name. From the house of your god I will destroy carved and cast images. I will make your burial, for they are swift.

target_units.text: I will destroy your carved images and pillars from your midst, and you will certainly no longer bow down to the works of your hands.

relationship: shared announcement of good news and peace upon the mountains
rationale: Nahum calls attention to the feet on the mountains of one bringing good news and announcing peace. Isaiah likewise combines mountains, feet, good news and a report of peace, alongside salvation and God's reign. The distinctive cluster of images directly connects the announcements.
source_text: Look, upon the mountains are the feet of one bringing good news and announcing peace! Celebrate your feasts, Judah; repay your vows. For they will no longer pass through you into decay. It has been completed; it has been removed.

target_units.text: like beauty on the mountains, like the feet of one proclaiming a report of peace, like one bringing good news. For I will make your salvation heard, saying, ‘Zion, your God will reign.’”

relationship: later scriptural use of the good-news messenger's feet
rationale: Nahum depicts the feet of one bringing good news and peace. Romans introduces written Scripture about the beautiful feet of those announcing good things within its discussion of sent proclaimers. The shared messenger image is retained without claiming Romans names Nahum as its source.
source_text: Look, upon the mountains are the feet of one bringing good news and announcing peace! Celebrate your feasts, Judah; repay your vows. For they will no longer pass through you into decay. It has been completed; it has been removed.

target_units.text: And how are they to proclaim unless they are sent? Just as it is written, “How beautiful are the feet of those announcing good things!”

relationship: the Lord's opposition to Jacob's arrogance
rationale: Nahum says the Lord turned away Jacob's arrogance, alongside Israel's arrogance and their ravaged vine branches. Amos likewise declares the Lord's abhorrence of all Jacob's arrogance before threatening the city. The connection preserves the native arrogance wording rather than substituting restoration of splendor.
source_text: because the Lord turned away Jacob’s arrogance, as Israel’s arrogance; for those shaking them out shook out both them and their vine branches; they ruined

target_units.text: For the Lord swore by Himself: “I abhor all Jacob’s arrogance and have hated his regions; I will remove the city with all who inhabit it.”

relationship: weapons broken within descriptions of destructive power
rationale: Nahum's sentence continues from 2:3 into the ruining of the weapons of might, followed by mighty men playing in fire and troubled horsemen. The psalm explicitly describes the Lord breaking a weapon apart and burning shields. The connection concerns ruined military equipment; it does not make the agents or every fire detail identical.
source_text: the weapons of their might from among people, mighty men playing in fire. The reins of their chariots are on the day of his preparation, and the horsemen will be thrown into uproar

target_units.text: Bringing wars to an end as far as the earth’s limits, He will shatter a bow and break a weapon apart and burn shields in fire.

relationship: chariots and fiery imagery in an advancing force
rationale: Nahum describes chariots in confused motion with an appearance like fire torches and flashing lightning. Joel compares the advancing force to horses and chariots and its sound to a fiery flame. Both combine swift military movement with fire imagery, using distinct descriptions.
source_text: in the roads, and the chariots will be thrown into confusion and entangled in the squares; their appearance is like torches of fire and lightning flashing past.

target_units.text: Their appearance is like the sight of horses; like riders they will pursue.
With a sound like chariots they will leap upon mountain peaks, like the sound of a fiery flame devouring stubble, like a numerous and strong people arrayed for war.

relationship: defensive preparations at city walls
rationale: Nahum describes nobles hurrying to the walls and preparing defenses amid weakness. Isaiah describes Jerusalem's houses pulled down to fortify the wall and water provided between walls. Both depict city defenses being prepared under threat, with different specified preparations.
source_text: Their nobles will remember and flee by day; they will weaken on their journey, hurry to the walls and prepare their defenses.

target_units.text: and uncover the hidden things of the houses in David’s citadel. They saw that they were many and that the old pool’s water had been diverted into the city,
and that Jerusalem’s houses had been pulled down to fortify the city’s wall.
You provided water for yourselves between the two walls, inside the old pool, and did not look to the One who made her from the beginning or see the One who founded her.

relationship: the plundering of a city's accumulated possessions
rationale: Nahum describes silver and gold being plundered amid abundant adornment and desirable vessels. Ezekiel's oracle against Tyre likewise announces the stripping of possessions and demolition of desirable houses. The connection concerns the seizure of urban wealth, without identifying the two cities.
source_text: They were plundering silver; they were plundering gold. There was no limit to her adornment; they have been weighed down beyond all her desirable vessels.

target_units.text: He will plunder your strength, strip your possessions, throw down your walls, and demolish your desirable houses. He will throw your stones, timber, and dust into the sea.
